## Bioconductor

[Bioconductor](https://www.bioconductor.org/) is a project which aims to develop and share open-source software for precise and repeatable analysis of biological data.
They foster an inclusive and collaborative community of developers and data scientists.

## Why Bioconductor?

- Analysis workflows are long and complex, an ecosystem of R packages for genomics data analysis facilitates reuse.
- Common data structures allow interoperability between packages.
- Package build system automates testing, ensures compatibility, and improves reproducibility.
- Community events and forums improve collaboration.

You can:

- Use high-quality, interoperable, and well-documented Bioconductor R packages.
- Develop and [contribute](https://contributions.bioconductor.org/bioconductor-package-submissions.html) your own R packages for genomics analysis.

## Accessing Bioconductor packages

You might typically install a package from CRAN through `install.packages()`. 
Bioconductor packages are hosted elsewhere and have a different mechanism for installing.

First, we'll install BiocManager from CRAN, and we can then use BiocManager to install packages from Bioconductor.

````{r eval=F}

## not required as packages installed through workshop package installation.
install.packages('BiocManager')
BiocManager::install('SingleCellExperiment')

````

You can then load packages as normal.

````{r message=F, warning=F}

library(SingleCellExperiment)
library(scrapper)
library(TENxPBMCData)

````

As well as hosting, testing, and distributing packages, Bioconductor also ships some core infrastructure which improves interoperability between packages.
These usually come in the form of data structures for storing different types of data.
In this workshop, we'll use the SingleCellExperiment class.

Data used are from the *4k PBMCs from a Healthy Donor* dataset released by 10x Genomics (2017),
distributed via the TENxPBMCData Bioconductor package.
The dataset contains approx. 4,000 cells from peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs).
These are mostly immune cells.

````{r}

sce<-TENxPBMCData::TENxPBMCData('pbmc4k')

citation("TENxPBMCData")

````

The SingleCellExperiment object keeps the different types of data relevant to our analysis neatly organised in one object.
Each data point is associated with a feature and an observation, but we might also want to keep other information, for example: 

- each feature (gene) can be named using different conventions, or have different aliases.
- each observation (cell) might need its patient ID, sequencing batch, quality metrics or cluster ID attached.

Being able to access data from this object is crucial for analysis.

````{r}

class(sce)

sce

counts(sce)[1:4,1:4] # subsetting on genes and cells respectively

head(colData(sce)) # accessing cell metadata

head(rowData(sce)) # accessing gene metadata

````

For convenience, column data (data describing the cells) can also be accessed using the '$' operator.

````{r}

table(sce$Individual)

````

We don't always work with the raw counts.
For example, normalised values reduce the impact of differences in sequencing depth, and are typically used for dimension reduction and clustering.

We can store transformations of the raw data, e.g. normalised counts, in assays.

````{r}

assays(sce)
sce<-scrapper::normalizeRnaCounts.se(sce) # can be access as logcounts(sce)
assays(sce)

````

Aaaand we can also store embeddings of the data, such as from PCA, TSNE or UMAP.

````{r}

reducedDimNames(sce) ## empty for now but we'll add to it later.

````

Finally, we can store alternative experiments, or modalities, which were measured on the same cells.
For example, [CITE-seq](https://emea.illumina.com/techniques/sequencing/rna-sequencing/cite-seq.html) data measures gene and surface protein expression simultaneously.

Why might we want to treat these separately rather than appending them to the main counts?
Well, different distribution (bimodal for CITE-seq) mean different preprocessing, but storing them in the one object allows for joint analysis down the line.

````{r}

altExpNames(sce) ## also expected to be empty for this workshop.

````
